title: Lesson 67: Voice Agents: STT, TTS, Latency, Interruptions, and Barge-In
description: How a voice agent is built from a streaming STT, LLM, and TTS pipeline, why the latency budget is the whole game, how turn detection decides when the user is done, and how barge-in lets a caller interrupt without the conversation derailing.

questions.question: Per lesson 67, why does the three-piece STT to LLM to TTS pipeline dominate production voice agents even though realtime speech-to-speech models exist?
options: Because speech-to-speech models are always more expensive, so the pipeline is the only affordable option
Because the LLM wants text, and the voice components translate audio into that token space and back, while measured open speech-to-speech models are still too slow for realtime interaction
Because the pipeline is the only architecture that supports any form of streaming
Because speech-to-speech models cannot produce natural prosody, so the pipeline is the only natural-sounding choice
questions.explanation: The lesson frames a voice agent as an LLM agent with voice I/O: the reasoning and tool use happen in the LLM's token space, which wants text, and the voice components translate audio in and out. It also cites the Salesforce measurement that Qwen2.5-Omni, a representative open speech-to-speech model, was too slow for realtime interaction at roughly 13 seconds of time-to-first-audio.

questions.question: A voice agent feels slow even though its LLM is fast. Following the lesson, what is the most likely cause and the correct fix?
options: The LLM is too small, so the fix is to use a larger model
The stages run sequentially instead of overlapping, so the fix is to stream partial transcripts into the LLM and stream partial text into TTS so nothing waits for a stage to fully finish
The TTS voice quality is too low, so the fix is to upgrade the voice
The STT model is too accurate, so the fix is to use a faster but less accurate one
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that the latency budget only closes when stages overlap: recognition emits words while the user is still speaking, the decision model is primed on the partial transcript, and streaming TTS speaks the first clause while the model generates the rest. A fast model alone does not fix a sluggish agent if endpointing or non-streaming synthesis keeps it slow.

questions.question: A caller says "yeah" while the agent is reading a long explanation, and the agent stops talking and treats it as a new request. Per lesson 67, what went wrong?
options: The agent's barge-in policy failed to classify the input as a backchannel, which should not cancel critical audio
The agent's echo cancellation was too aggressive and removed the caller's speech
The agent's STT model had too high a word error rate on the word "yeah"
The agent's turn detection was set to model-based, which is always wrong for short inputs
questions.explanation: The lesson treats barge-in as a policy, not a toggle, and classifies each input: a caller saying "yeah" while listening is a backchannel that should usually not interrupt, while a true correction like "no, I meant Friday" should. A false barge-in that stops for a backchannel is more damaging than a missed one.
